newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief questions abandoning troops for Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief questions abandoning troops for Zaire.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Thursday said dropping plans for an international force to rescue refugees in eastern Zaire was premature.
"In retrospect the multinational force should not have been disbanded," Annan told a news conference. He said it probably should be suspended in order to be activated at a later date if needed.
"In the absence of the willing and the will, there is little the United Nations can do in terms of putting in a force to help stranded refugees," he said.

Plans for a force organised by Canada were abandoned in December after refugees began to return to Rwanda from Zaire amid a revolt against the Zairean government. The United States and others disputed U.N. figures about how many refugees were trapped in Zaire.
But Annan cautioned that if a force needed to be put together again some kind of ceasefire would have to be in effect -- one aim of U.N. envoy Mohammed Sahnoun who expects to visit Zaire this week.

Queried about elections the Zairean government wants to hold in July, Annan said the United Nations had been asked to give assistance and an election team, to be joined shortly by Sahnoun, was in Zaire at the moment.
"There is a question here of financing, there is a question of assistance, there is a legal question," he said. "And I wonder whether we can resolve all of these problems before July.
"There is also a question of whether we can organise an election in a country where a war is going on. That problem too has to be resolved."

Annan, who took office on Jan. 1, said Sahnoun would try to get all parties to the negotiating table. "Once they are at the table and we begin to talk we hope that we can convince all the parties in Zaire to accept participation in the election as the ultimate solution to their differences."

The government under Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo wants to hold elections in July but opposition groups charge they could not be conducted fairly. At the same time Kengo and his government have staked their reputation on a military solution to the war, which began when rebels took up arms in October, accusing Zairean authorities of denying them citizenship.

With President Mobutu Sese Seko suffering from cancer, France and Belgium are said to be particularly anxious that elections be held to rescue whatever institutions remain in a collapsing state. Under Mobutu, Zaire's infrastructure deteriorated, entire regions became virtually autonomous and the economy was shattered despite its mining exports.
